title: Chevra Kadisha: True Kindness
hook: volunteers who prepare the body for burial
carry: kindness to the dead is true kindness

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was shomer, the one in the chair through the night, and your line was the dead are honored, never left alone. Today, the people who come in the morning.
screen: `THE DEAD ARE HONORED, NEVER LEFT ALONE.`

segments.voice: "Deal kindly and truly with me." Jacob says it near the end of Genesis, old and dying in Egypt, to his son Joseph. His request is specific: don't bury me here. Carry me home, and lay me with my fathers. Joseph swears he will. Notice what Jacob asks for. Not money, not a blessing. A burial done right, by someone he trusts, after he can no longer say thank you. Jewish communities built a whole institution around that request.
screen: `DEAL KINDLY AND TRULY WITH ME.` → `BURY ME WITH MY FATHERS.` → `HE CAN NEVER SAY THANK YOU.`

segments.voice: It's called the chevra kadisha. Chevra means a society, a group of companions; kadisha is Aramaic for holy. The holy society prepares a body for burial: washing it, dressing it, placing it in the coffin. They are usually volunteers, ordinary people, a teacher, a dentist, a retired bus driver, who answer the phone when someone dies. Women care for women and men for men. You met Jacob's words in your first year. The commentator Rashi, reading them, says kindness done for the dead is true kindness, chesed shel emet, because the one receiving it can never repay. No thanks, no favor returned, no one to impress. At the end of Deuteronomy, Moses dies on a mountain, and the text says he was buried there, and that no one knows his grave. The rabbis read it as God himself burying Moses. So, they teach, as God buries the dead, so should you. The holy society does what the tradition calls divine work, with rubber gloves and a basin. Some societies keep a yearly day of their own, linked to the memory of Moses, with a fast and then a meal together. The rest of the year, the work is quiet. A society is holy not because of who joins, but because of what it does for people who can't ask.
screen: `VOLUNTEERS WHO ANSWER THE PHONE.` · `TRUE KINDNESS: NO REPAYMENT.` · `GOD BURIED MOSES.` · `HOLY BECAUSE OF THE WORK.` · then, large: `CHEVRA KADISHA: TRUE KINDNESS.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind people who do work few people see: hospice volunteers, night-shift nurses, whoever washed the dishes at the last funeral you went to. Picture one of their faces and thank them silently, by name if you know it. If you pray, you can pray for them.
Chevra kadisha. The holy society: volunteers who prepare the dead for burial, doing true kindness that can never be repaid. Today's word.
Your line: kindness to the dead is true kindness. It can never be repaid. That's today, done.

howItsDone: Jewish communities may have a chevra kadisha, a burial society of volunteers who prepare the body for burial, with women caring for women and men for men; some also arrange the shemira and help the family with the funeral.
